searchText: Could you please give more context on that? What is the desirable property of a system or approach you're looking for? Tx rewards will be toped up with the same coinbase mechanism as before the merge. The question is who sets the coinbase address for particular execution payload. And whom do we want to give an ability to set it. It could be set once at the launch of execution client and never changed after or it could be send by beacon chain client that is being produced a block each time it does it. The former doesn't require any additional work, the latter would require adding coinbase address to `assembleBlock` params which is doable. But the latter would work well only in a trusted setup. Because execution client may set whatever address to the coinbase it would want to and beacon chain client have only one way to react, it either uses the payload with the coinbase address in it or falls back to an empty payload. Sharing fees between these two parties is more sophisticated but also doable, execution client may set coinbase to its own address and include transaction that transfers a portion of fees in a block -- the tricky part for a beacon client would be to verify this transfer. It'd be desirable for the beacon chain / consensus client to be able to signal this to the execution client on a block-per-block basis. I am thinking of infrastructure providers like Blox Staking. They run centralized execution clients and consensus clients, and their users run remote signers in their own AWS instances. They've expressed a desire to have a mapping of validator public key to desired `coinbase` payout address, which would be controlled by the user, and have the priority fees go directly to their user/customer on each block. They don't want to be custodians of that and then have to figure out how to split it up. That is a trusted setup in this case, as they control both the execution client and the consensus client. Then they will have to store mapping of validator pub-key/index on addresses and have a kind of proxy that would pick the right address depending on proposer index/pub-key and send it to execution client on `assembleBlock` request. Or extend consensus API with a new method that matches validators onto coinbase addresses and patch their execution client's code. I we say that: - small stakers are good for decentralization - tx rewards can vary a lot from block to block (also, MEV stuff) - small stakers don't like unpredictable/random rewards (they prefer a more stable income) So I'm a bit afraid that varying rewards will push new and existing small stakers to use more centralized solutions like staking pools instead, for the sake of predictable (or higher) income. I was hoping for a shade of gray where small stakers can still stake themselves, but can delegate and/or share block production/coinbase rewards somewhat trustlessly/decentralized. You mean that pool may offer tx fee shares independently on the number of produced blocks by each validator but on some different conditions, like on per ETH staked basis making tx fees income more stable hence more attractive for individual stakers? A system based on the number of block proposals would already be smoother than not pooling I think, but what you describe is even smoother (and therefore "more attractive") yes. Individual stakers may propose on their own and grab transaction fees. What pool can done for them is to take a portion of fee for running the execution client for them which might be also appealing depending on how resourceful is to run own execution client That's why my question above: if the operator is willing to run on a pool, pools can enforce using of a coinbase to a contract that will later distribute ETH from tx fees to all operators. Without staking on a pool I think delayed methods should be simple: you sign in a "coimbase pool" and set your coinbase to their contract. After n months that contact redistributes everything they got to their subscribers, checking that all their blocks were sent to the contract For the beacon chain we would have solo stakers, decentralized pooling like RocketPool, trustless SSV staking, and centralized staking (probably more shades). For the exec layer we would have... Solo/individual nodes, and centralized pools (e.g. single geth node that everyone subscribes/listens to). Wouldn't you just be selfish, and if a 10 ETH tx reward block reward come along just take the lot (set coinbase to your own address)? Only if tx reward is about average (or lower than average) does it make sense to send it to the pool. I suppose so, but if the n months is large enough to expect several blocks in that timeframe, the game for the single staker is more complicated Depends on the payout method as well I guess. If it's based on # proposals or ETH staked. Anyway, I'd rather have something that is _not_ susceptible to such selfish behavior (but still encourages people to run their own exec layer node). We're discussing this a lot in the rocketpool server as well Apologies for the unrelated question: I see discussions that Ropstein and other testnets will be forked to accept 1559 soon. Are there any plans to deploy a contract there and start a public testnet there so that we can merge it? Are any of those public execution testnets expendable? I also think this is a big problem and especially for a fully decentralized/trustless/nonpermissioned solution (where e.g. node operators are running their own execution clients) I'd choose it to be dependent on staked eth and the time you staked it, completely independent on block production, since you want to socialize luck You basically need a penalization mechanism and in certain cases of MEV rewards even the penalization mechanism may be worthless (e.g. imagine if EV extractable from 1 block is > 16 eth, which is the required deposit from a node operator) I understand why we want to use the coinbase address pre-merge and until withdrawals are enabled, but post-merge, post-withdrawals, why can't EV rewards go to the staking reward address instead? In the case of pools can't you force your operators to run signed, untampered software? If you control their clients you can set coinbase Is it a technical "this is not really possible issue due to how the execution chain and beacon chain operate" or is it a "we haven't seen a reason to do the work to make this possible"? How would you force your operators to run signed software? Also if it's simply a mater of configuring the a parameter for the client, how do you enforce a specific configuration? In the case of LIDO where it's permissioned in theory you can (if a staking pool operator goes rogue you can depermission them). In rocketpool you can't I mean to sign in your pool you need to run a pool provided software, that software sends proof that it's untampered every attestation or every epoch or whatever period. If your see this failing you punish the operator yes but there's cases where the maximum punishment may be less than the value extracted for going rogue in which case the punishment is useless <@!77492786336636928> I am understanding you correctly that you think this "problem" would be solved if rewards go to the validator balance? It can, be because this validator address can be a smart contract (I haven't thought about it as much, and I didn't see it mentioned a lot here yet either, which is why I started the conversation) and the stipulation would be that the "rewards address" is assigned at creation and cannot be changed by the node operator It is very hard to go rogue in that scenario: your user will have to be running two sets of beacons constantly: one tampered and one untampered, and if he sees a block worth more than 16ETH then switch. If you are enforcing coinbase to be a contract you control You really can't enforce that when the node operator is running their own client, though even this "anti-tampering" mechanism doesn't work, you jsut increase the possible cost so basically the "go or don't go rogue" equation changes from `(1 time MEV reward) > (operator's staked ETH)` to is `(1 time MEV reward) > (operator's staked ETH + deferred rewards not yet distributed)` correct If there's a technical solution to be had I think it's better to consider it than to rely on this cost/benefit mechanism, because we really have no way to be able to tell how large these MEV rewards may get I don't think you will see even after the merge rewards going directly to the validator's balance. However I think you can send it to the withdrawal address which may be useful for pools like yours and this can be done right at the merge without any changes but if you mean to "get rid of coinbase mechanism" You mean the node operator can choose to point the coinbase address to the withdrawal address, but the problem with that is the enforcement mechanism (which we discussed above) But im saying, replace the coinbase mechanism Yes, that's something that I expect eventually will be gone I get why we don't want to do it now It does not make sense at least to me, to keep it and I get why we don't want to do it until withdrawals are enabled at the very soonest... but if it's technically feasible it would solve a lot of issues even now, in an ugly fashion, but at the protocol level you could enforce this, by ignoring coinbase if the proposer has an eth1 withrawal prefix the problem is that the distribution of that eth is done by the execution engine, which does not have knowledge of the beaconchain Will this "always" be true? Like is there some way/plans in the future for the execution engine to have knowledge of the beaconchain? I don't know the answer to this. Ways I suspect there are, specially if we ever move to execution shards, as for plans, I only suspects there are none for the time being. The execution engine has _some_ knowledge of the beaconchain (at least in the full merge) as it will have access to the Randao mix and the beaconstate root through opcodes For software running on untrusted hardware, this is not possible. Under this scenario, any software (with more or less effort) can be reverse engineered and send fake integrity checks. When the time is right (e.g. a sufficient MEV reward appears) then the attacker changes the coinbase address. This is just a simple “if” in the code We could enforce withdrawal address set to the coinbase on the protoc
